Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language names, just like in spoken language, have a conventionalised form in the sense that a community of signers will recognize them, and people know that that is that person's name. But there's no rule on how you form them. You can base it on facial features, on behaviour, on personality, or even on a funny anecdote, or you can base it on the phonology of the person's spoken language name. So, for example, here in Denmark I have a friend whose name is John, and his sign name is based on the phonology of the English pronunciation of John. So it's just a name that is loosely connected to the spoken language name. Other people's sign names have nothing to do with their spoken language name. And then there's also what we call self-names, where the person herself has chosen a sign name. And then there are generic names, where for example, you give a woman who is short, brown, has curly hair, a generic name that could belong to any woman who looks like that, so you use that for her until you know her better.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Names in sign language are quite unique. Every sign name is very idiosyncratic and personal. It is usually associated with something about the person, maybe their appearance, but it could also be a behavior, a personality trait, or a famous movie character or actor or whatever. But also sometimes names just develop out of the context of the sign name, the sign name of their parent or their friend or their romantic partner. So sign names are very different than spoken names in the sense that they are not hierarchical, they are not given by parents. They are very fluid, they are very changeable, people can change their sign name when they move to a new city, they might get a new sign name. They might even have different sign names for different friend groups. Sign names are often derived from visual features, but they can also be conceptual. So if someone is very funny, for example, they might get a sign name for clown.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language has its own way of making names. It's not just the fingerspelling of English names or whatever the language of the country. There's a kind of iconic naming system where if, say, you have a huge head, you might get the sign for giant head or big head. And so these are iconic names. And the hand shape or the location of the sign or the movement of the sign will represent something about the person's appearance or personality. Those are called descriptive names. But then there are also arbitrary names where it's not related to the person at all. And the interesting thing is that signers will have multiple names. They will have a name in a certain group of friends, another name in another group of friends, and in a family, they might have yet another name. So names are context-dependent and group-dependent. And if you work in a deaf community, you might actually have the impression that there's 100 names of the same person. And that is very, very normal in sign language.

Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for your question, it's interesting. Well, mammals, they drink sea water but they have this organ in the kidney that is called the salt gland, or in some species it's in the nasal passages. It produces very salty urine and it gets rid of the salts, so they do drink sea water, they can, and they also eat prey that is rich in water. So most marine mammals are able to get water from the sea and from prey.

There are also some marine mammals that are very dependent on prey for water, for example the penguins. They cannot drink sea water, but they drink the water that is contained in the fish that they eat. So it depends. But the basic principle for the ocean mammals is that they can drink sea water and they have a very efficient mechanism in the kidneys that separates the salt from the water and they retain the water and they excrete the salt. But again it's not universal, it's not true for every mammal, but it's very widespread.

So in general, yes, they can drink sea water. And they can drink really very salty water, much saltier than sea water, even in some cases. Like some whales can drink very very salty water. But some species, like the penguins, no.

Anyway, I hope that answers your question.

Cheers,
Alex

Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi there,

Great to hear from you, hope you are well. I love that you are asking science questions these days.

Anyway, marine mammals, so seals, sea lions, sea otters, whales, dolphins, porpoises, etc. actually do need to drink water. They need to drink it to replenish the salts they get from their prey. So for instance, a seal will drink more salt water and then its kidneys filter out the salts, the excess salts, and produce very concentrated urine. So it's a very efficient process. And that's why seal urine smells so bad, very concentrated urine. So the mammals are replenishing the salts, but they're drinking too much water. So they have to filter out the water as well. And they do that very efficiently, especially the marine mammals. We call them euryhaline mammals, they can adapt very well to different salinity. So that's how they hydrate. But some whales, for example, they don't drink any water at all. They get all their water from their prey. And the reason is that they feed at a very low trophic level, so they're feeding on krill, on copepods, or on very small fish, and those organisms actually contain very little salt. So that's why they don't need to drink. And if I have a question for you, actually, I will need some help with my fruit trees. Is it over there? Anyway, let's meet soon and talk.

Cheers,
Yann

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: Child support is based on income because in most cases, we don't know precisely how much is necessary for the child and that's going to vary widely. A child in Hawaii or in Manhattan is going to have a very different cost of living than a child in rural Vermont, so it would be very difficult to set a global rule for what children need. Income is very easy to obtain. People generally report it, they have tax returns, they can prove it. Needs are very subjective and they are very variable. So we use a proxy, which is income. And the proxy works pretty well because in general the more affluent a family is, the more expensive the child is. So it's a good approximation. The problem is that it fails in the extreme cases. So the case where you have a really expensive child but not very affluent parents. In that case, it's going to be very difficult for the parents to meet the child's needs. And then in the other extreme, a very affluent parent and a child that's very simple, that doesn't need much, that's going to be really overkill. But overall it works pretty well.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: The reason is that the cost of a child is a very difficult thing to objectively define. What is a "reasonable" amount for a child, what are reasonable activities, reasonable clothes, reasonable housing, reasonable food, what quality of life do we think the child should have. It's very subjective and also the income is a much more objective measurement. So in most jurisdictions, they look at the income of the parents, and they use some kind of formula or table to determine what the payment is. So that reduces some of the subjectivity. And then after that, if there is a dispute, then it can be altered up or down based on special circumstances. For example, a child that has special medical needs, it's very likely that the payment will be higher. So in general, it's a heuristic that works well in practice, but then there is some flexibility. And if you know the methodology that is used in your jurisdiction, you can always argue that the payment should be increased or reduced based on the needs of the child.

And of course, in special circumstances, a court can deviate from the guidelines and adjust the amount up or down. But in the standard case, I think income-based is better.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw: I think the popcorn kernel is a remarkable little pressure cooker, and I think we should just take a moment to appreciate the physics and chemistry of that tiny kernel. It's really one of my favorite things to look at. When it pops, I think the most interesting thing is that it's a pressure vessel. It's a hard outer shell, very hard, and inside is this starchy endosperm that's very dry. There's not much moisture in it, but there is some. So when you heat it up, that moisture turns to steam and that steam has no place to go because the outer shell is so hard and so thick. So it's just building and building pressure. Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw: I think there's a misconception that popcorn popping is just an explosion, which is a little reductive. I think what's happening is a very slow pressurization of a very small water droplet, which is basically trapped in this dense little hull of a kernel. So the water inside is actually sealed and it's liquid, and as you heat it up it becomes superheated. So it's above 100 degrees, and it's still in liquid state because of the pressure that's building up. So as it continues to heat up, the pressure inside goes up and up and up until it reaches the breaking point of the hull. And then the hull just breaks and the steam inside expands and turns to gas. And as it turns to gas, it expands, it takes up space, and it's going to expand by about 40 times its volume. So that's what's actually happening. The explosion is just the moment of the breaking. But the popping is just the expansion of the water into a gas and it expands inside, but it's also expanding the starch inside. The starch is gelatinized. It's kind of like a dough. And then it expands. And then once it cools down, it sets in that state. So it's not just a piece of water balloon that breaks. It's really the whole structure of the kernel that expands and then sets into that foamy substance that we call popcorn. And there are a lot of things that make the pop better, or make it more fluffy. The starch structure is very important. What type of starch do you have inside the kernel. If you have more amylose, more amylopectin, it's going to give you a different shape. The harder the hull, the more pressure you can build up before it breaks, and the more pressure you build up, the more it's going to expand. So the kernel is a really complicated tiny little container that is designed to pop. And that's actually pretty amazing. Every time I see a cornfield, I think, that's very nice. I will get my snacks from that. Every single one of these kernels is designed to go through this process, this transformation. And it's amazing to me. And I think popcorn is one of my favorite foods. I can eat a bucket of popcorn, my size, in one sitting. But it's the movie popcorn that I like. Like with the butter and the salt, that I like. Not the ones that are too oily, too salty, that are too sweet, that have the caramel and that are too chewy. I don't like that. I like the crisp, fluffy, buttery popcorn.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw:
I think popcorn is one of the most interesting phenomena in the natural world. We can actually witness, with a little bit of suspense, a solid changing state to a gas, changing state to solid again, in a way that just seems magical. There is no chemical reaction going on. The popcorn is not being burned or oxidized or anything like that. All that is happening is a very interesting physical change of state of the water molecules inside the kernel of corn.

The popcorn is actually a seed, and it's a seed that contains starch and proteins and other things, but also contains a small amount of water. So the water is in the liquid state, but it's inside the starch, which is a solid, and the starch is solid because it has been dried out. So we have this water in the liquid state, but it's in a sort of a gel inside this solid. This is all at room temperature, and the kernel is hard and very durable. You can bite it with your teeth and it's very hard.

When you put the kernel into a pot and start heating it, the water inside starts to turn into vapor. The kernel is very hard, and it has a very strong shell, the pericarp. And inside the kernel there is a small chamber where there is a higher concentration of water. And as the water turns into vapor, the pressure inside the kernel increases. And it can increase to enormous pressures. Like 10 times the atmospheric pressure or more. The kernel is very good at resisting that pressure, but eventually it breaks. And when it breaks, it breaks explosively. The pressure is released and the water vaporizes very quickly, and as it vaporizes, it takes a lot of energy, and as it takes energy it cools the starch very quickly. And the starch, which was a very amorphous gel, turns into a solid very quickly.

And because it cools so quickly, the starch molecules don't have time to get together and form a crystalline solid, like a regular solid. Instead, it forms a glassy solid. It's like glass. It's just solidified without crystallizing. And what happens is that the water vapor pushes the starch molecules very quickly, and the starch solidifies around that water vapor. So you end up with a solid glassy starch that has a lot of empty volume inside, which is why it's so light. So, it's a little bit of the same principle of a soufflé, where you have air bubbles inside, but this time it's a glassy solid. It's very stable and very light, and it's also porous. And that's why when you put butter or salt or sugar on it, it sticks to it very well, because it's very porous. So the kernel is just a little pressure cooker that breaks, and when it breaks, it forms a solid glassy material. And that's popcorn.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

Question: Why is the history of math so separated from math itself in education? Wouldn't it be more interesting if this weren't the case?
items.raw:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for your message. Great question. I think there's a good reason it's separated, and it's because in maths, there's a very special pedagogical framework that's hard to break, which is that we learn from basics and then go up in complexity. So we start with arithmetic, then algebra, then analysis, then the differential equations, etc. So I think it's difficult to embed the history of math in the main stream of maths learning, but I don't think it's impossible. It's just more difficult to do. I think the math historians do a very good job in keeping them separate, but I think if you really want to motivate students, the best thing is to start from the historical motivation and go into the actual maths. So instead of saying, look, this is a theorem that says this and that, it's more interesting to say, look, in the 16th century, the mathematicians were really puzzled by this problem and then they came up with this way of solving it. And I think that's very, very powerful. But I think it's very difficult to do it at all stages of education. Anyway, I think it's a really good idea and I hope it's more and more integrated in the future.

Cheers,
Miles

Question: Why does metal react so violently when microwaved?
items.raw: When metal is microwaved, the electric field from the microwave causes free electrons in the metal to move about randomly, or jiggle. A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I think there's two factors at play here. The first is cultural and the second is actuarial. In terms of culture, the USA is a country that has a very special relationship with alcohol. In many other countries, they drink wine or beer with their meals and it's very normalized. In the US, people drink in bars. People go to bars, and they have a tendency to get drunk. So people are more concerned about drinking and driving and various other things. So the drinking age is lower in Europe and other countries because the drinking culture is more about sipping a beer or wine at a restaurant. Whereas in the US it's more about going to bars and having a huge number of drinks over a few hours. That's one factor. The second factor is that when they set the drinking age, they looked at the actuarial data on accidents and mortality and such, and they found that there was a massive jump in accidents, in deaths, and in other bad outcomes at age 21. So they just decided that the actuarial data says we should set it at 21. This is in contrast to the rest of the world, where most countries have set it at 18, and a few set it at 19. So it is very much an American quirk. And then the driving age, it's interestingly, is not uniform across the states. Some states are 18, some states are 16, some states are 17, and so on. So the driving age is not that great an argument. But the drinking age is set at 21 uniformly across all the states, so it's more uniform, and it's more of a problem. I think that the drinking age in America should be lowered to 18, because I think it's a differentiating factor that is creating a lot of bad outcomes. For example, young people go to college, and they're supposed to be adults, they can vote, they can join the army, they can be drafted, and so on, but they can't go and buy a beer in a store. So they just get very creative and sneaky. They end up bringing homegrown ID cards or fake ID cards or something like that, and they just drink. And they drink a lot more than people who are in countries where they can legally buy alcohol. So it's very silly, and I think the culture of alcohol in the US is definitely something that needs to change.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I think it is a bizarre compromise. It's a bit of a stupid law. The drinking age in the US, 21, was set back in 1984, so almost 40 years ago. Before that it was all over the place, the states were different. Some states had 18, some states had 19, some 20, some 21, some 22. And so it was a very confusing situation for the country. And then there was this national campaign, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, MADD, who wanted to lower the drinking age to 18. This is the side of it that people don't really know. They didn't want to raise the age, they wanted to lower the age to 18. And so they managed to get the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the NHTSA, to create a grant. That is, if a state were to lower the drinking age to 21, they would give them some grant money, some federal money. That was a pretty straightforward deal. 10% of the federal grants that were given for highways. If you had the drinking age at 18, then you would lose 10% of your federal grants. And so a lot of states wanted to retain those grants. So they moved the age to 21. And then, a few years later, Congress just made it mandatory. So that's why we have 21. It's purely political. It's not medical. It's not scientific. There's nothing that suggests that you become sober at 21. There's nothing that suggests that we should treat a 20 year old differently than a 21 year old. And the reason why they settled on 21 and not 22 is that the US was already a military power, and they were deploying soldiers to Vietnam and to other places. And their soldiers were 18 to 20, and they didn't want to make them drink beer only in the barracks. They wanted to be able to go to the pubs with their buddies in France or in Korea and drink beer. And that's why they settled on 21. So it's a very weird compromise, but now it's very hard to move it. Even though the drinking age in the US is 21, the legal drinking age, the alcohol consumption in the US is very high. So it's not like a really effective law.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I think we're a bit spoiled in the US because we are the country that invented the car and then decided to regulate alcohol consumption using the car as a proxy. A lot of it is just a holdover of cultural stuff. The alcohol culture in the United States is not a very tolerant one. We tend to be kind of a teetotaler culture, and it tends to be very extreme in its approach. So the idea is that if we don't let people drink until they are older, we'll reduce the likelihood that young people will have terrible accidents. And the research is mixed on that. Some research shows that the death rate goes up among young people if you raise the age of drinking. In particular, they drink more heavily and they may even take more risks if they don't get access to alcohol in a controlled way. But then there's research that shows that the accident rate goes down. The safety is in the statistics, and it's very hard to tease out what is a factor that is going to cause a car crash. How much alcohol you're drinking, what type of alcohol, what kind of car, what kind of road, what kind of terrain, what time of day, are there other people in the car. And so I think that statistically it has been shown that if you go up to 21, the crash rate goes down. So in that sense, it's a very rational decision. But I think it's a very cultural thing, and there are other countries that also have a drinking age of 21. So it's not just the United States. And I think that the United States being a teetotaler culture, where you drink very strong stuff, very little water, and you very, very strongly dislike drunkenness. You either don't drink or you drink very hard. So we've decided that the only way to keep that in control is to delay it as long as possible. That's one theory. Another theory, and this is a little bit more of a pseudo-economic one, is that we want to have people with more money to buy alcohol, and 21 is a more typical age where people get a job and can afford to go to a bar or go to a nice restaurant and buy expensive wines and cocktails. And that's just my speculation, but I do think that's part of the culture in the United States. We just want people to be older and to have more money before they drink.

Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw: Tornado, hurricane, typhoon, cyclone, and similar words all refer to a storm with rotating winds and a low-pressure centre. The distinction is geographical or sometimes the shape of the storm. So, a hurricane is a very large tropical cyclone that forms over the Atlantic Ocean or the Northeast Pacific Ocean. Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw: These are all rotating weather systems, and in fact they are basically the same phenomena. Just at different locations and in different intensities. So, in the northern hemisphere, we call it a cyclone, in the southern hemisphere, an anti-cyclone. So, in the Pacific, it's called a typhoon, in the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean, it's called a hurricane. Then there's tropical storms and depressions, which are just weaker, less intense versions of these cyclones. And tornadoes, they're very much related, but they're actually different. Tornadoes are much smaller, much more intense, they're rotating columns of air, and can be very deadly and destructive. They're just very small, very intense vortexes, that are in fact usually attached to a thunderstorm, a cumulonimbus cloud, and they develop within it. So, tornadoes are much smaller, and much more intense, and they are related to thunderstorms. Cyclones, hurricanes, typhoons, they are much larger, they span across hundreds of kilometres, and they are actually big slow-moving rotating masses of air and clouds. They develop over warm tropical waters. And they get their energy from the warm waters. They actually suck in warm moist air from the surface, and then in the middle, in the eye of the cyclone, this air actually sinks, it gets compressed, it gets warmer, and then it rises. So it creates a very strong circulation, very strong winds. And then it also generates a lot of rain, very heavy rain, which is why they're very deadly, very dangerous, because they bring very strong winds and heavy rainfall. And they're very slow-moving, so they can stay in the same place for days, and bring heavy rain in the same region, which can lead to massive flooding. Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw:
Tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons, and tropical depressions are all intense atmospheric phenomena, but they differ in scale, location, and the energy that drives them. We first need to distinguish the smaller scale tornadoes from the much larger tropical cyclones. Tornadoes are the smallest and perhaps most violent of these phenomena. They are rotating columns of air extending from a thunderstorm down to the ground. The energy of a tornado comes from the violent updrafts and the shear that we have in thunderstorms. Their scale is relatively small; they're less than a few kilometres across, and they only last minutes to a few hours. They don't form in the ocean; they form over land, mostly over North America, but they can form anywhere in the world, including Australia, where we get tornadoes too. Tornadoes are not very predictable. They are very difficult to predict, and they can form very quickly, so that is one of the most dangerous aspects of tornadoes.

Then we have tropical cyclones. They are much larger, they're hundreds of kilometres across, and they last days. The energy of a tropical cyclone comes from the warm ocean surface, so we need warm water in the ocean, and in particular near the surface. They only form over the ocean, so they are not a land phenomenon. They can move inland, but they will decay quite rapidly once they move inland. Tropical cyclones have a very organised structure, with a low pressure centre and a calm centre called the eye. And then around the eye, you have very strong winds and a lot of rain. So the structure of a tropical cyclone is much more organised than a tornado.

So why do we have different names for tropical cyclones? So we have tropical cyclone, typhoon, hurricane, tropical depression, tropical storm, severe tropical storm. That's just a geographical location. So in the North Atlantic and the North-East Pacific, we call them hurricanes. In the North-West Pacific, we call them typhoons. And then in the Southern Hemisphere, we just call them tropical cyclones. The criteria for each category are the same. The only difference is the location. So a tropical depression will become a tropical storm when the wind speeds are above 63 kilometres per hour. It will become a severe tropical storm or a hurricane or a typhoon when the wind speeds are above 88 kilometres per hour. Then the higher categories of hurricane, typhoon, tropical cyclone are just how much wind speed you have. So a category 5 hurricane or a category 5 typhoon is the same thing. It's just a system that has very high sustained winds. And this is just a scale that we use, that has been established by the meteorological agencies. There is no sudden difference between a category 4 and a category 5. It's just how strong the winds are that determine the category of the cyclone.

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw: I think people sometimes abuse the term "white" to mean "generous" or "kind" or "nice". They mean it in a good way. But I hate that phrase because it has a very particular meaning. I think when someone says "that was mighty white of ya", they mean you did something that was nice or generous but in a way that was awkward or awkwardly generous or generous to the point of awkwardness. So for example, someone who goes to your house and then he sees that the fridge is empty and he leaves and comes back with a bunch of food and all kinds of groceries and puts them in your fridge and says "I hope you like them. Good luck." And then leaves without even introducing himself or his name or anything. That's white. That's not only nice and generous, but also very awkward. And it's a term that comes from a particular class, I think, of people in the United States, a middle class or lower middle class, in the South, and in the Midwest. There's a very particular kind of person, the white folks, in the cultural imagination, that is very nice, very generous, but at the same time doesn't quite know how to express themselves, is a little bit awkward and clumsy. So if I see that someone does a nice thing that is also a bit awkward, I'll say, "that's pretty white of you." But I don't think that it's purely nice. It's not purely nice. When you do something purely nice, you just do it in a very elegant way, and you don't feel awkward, and you don't even think that you did something nice, you just did it, and you left. So I think "white" has a little bit of awkwardness, a little bit of "I hope I did the right thing. I hope that you don't think I'm weird or something." That's what I think it means. And I don't think that the person who used the term towards me necessarily meant it in a negative way, but I just think that it's not purely nice.

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw:
I think this phrase is a very modern, affectionate way of saying "that was very kind of you" but with a slightly playful, exaggerated tone that might poke fun at how grand or self-sacrificing the gesture was. I don't think it's necessarily an accusation of racism, that it's a stereotype. I think it's like saying "you are so nice it's funny" or "you're too nice for your own good." So if I were a friend and I did something extra nice or self-sacrificing, say, I stay up all night to help my friend who is sick, maybe I just cook her food and stay there so that she doesn't have to move and do anything, and she says that, I just take it as a compliment. That was nice, but also funny because you went overboard.

I know the phrase might have been coined by a white person, but I don't think it's just a white person's saying. I think it has become part of the common language. I don't really notice a ton of the joke being at the expense of white people. I just notice it's said to anyone who does something nice. It's not necessarily derogatory. I don't want to go into the territory of saying who can say what, or what specific phrase is safe for whom and who should say it. But I feel like it's an overused phrase, and that's why it does become a little bit annoying or obnoxious sometimes. Because everyone says it. So, I do believe that it does have the connotation of maybe being slightly rude or funny. Like, "Oh, you're so nice, that's so white of you." And then they come back and say, "Oh, I'm so sorry, that was a weird joke, but I just meant you're so nice." And then maybe the person feels a little bit offended. So I think it's an affectionate phrase, but it's very close to the line of being a bit obnoxious. So I just try to use it sparingly.

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw: I think it's a very nice expression that we have in English. White. It's sort of a rarity in English to have an adjective that means goodness. Like, when you look at the color palette of English, most of them carry negative connotations. Black is bad, grey is bad, brown is bad, green is a bit weird. And then suddenly you have white, and it means nice, it means kind, it means moral. So I like it. It's a phrase I use myself. I think, the interesting thing is that it's a phrase that I think conveys purity of intention. It doesn't necessarily mean that the result of the action is good, it's not necessarily that the outcome was good. What it means is that the person had a good intention, that they were pure in what they did, that they didn't do it for selfish reasons, that they did it out of kindness, that they did it out of the goodness of their heart. It's not necessarily that they achieved the right thing, or that the outcome was what was expected. So I think that's what I like about it. I just wanted to help her out of kindness, and I thought it was an appropriate phrase to use. So yeah, it's nice.

That's not objective. That's culturally produced. That's just how we see the world, but we might perceive it differently. So, postmodernism is saying that all of our realities, all of our truths, are just in the same way, culturally produced. I think people get post-modernism all wrong. They think it means that nothing matters or that there's no truth or that there's no order. But I actually think it's just a very healthy, more human philosophy than the one that came before it. So the philosophy that came before it, modernism, is the philosophy of progress. The idea that we're always getting better and better. We're going up and up and up, always, ever, eternally. That we are becoming more and more rational, more and more scientific, more and more logical. And we're going to arrive at the utopia, the end of history. That's the modernist vision. And I think post-modernism just rejects that idea. It rejects the idea that there is just one ultimate truth, one ultimate society, one ultimate form of life. It's just saying that there are many truths, many societies, many forms of life, and they are all legit and none of them are superior to the other. That's really all it is. It's just a really healthy view of the world.

And in art, it's really fun. In modernism, art was really self-important. Modern art is like, we're the vanguard, we're the elite. We're the ones who are going to bring us into the future. Modern art is really elitist. It's very serious. It wants to be understood. It wants to have a message. Modern art really wants to send a message. And post-modern art just says, nah, I don't really want to send a message. I just want to be funny. I just want to be playful. I just want to be ironic. I just want to be a game. I want to mix different things together. I want to reference something that is high culture with something that is low culture, and I want to mix them together in a silly way. And that's really fun. In post-modern art, for example, you'll see a painting that has the Mona Lisa with a smiley face on it, or a painting that's very technical and very precise, but it depicts something silly, like a banana peel. You'll see things that are very ironic and very playful. It's more fun to me than the seriousness of modernism.

And in literature, in post-modern literature, for example, you have the novel Infinite Jest by David Foster Wallace. And it's a very good novel. It's very funny, very ironic, very playful. And it's also very erudite, very cultured. It's very deeply self-aware. It's very playful about the art of making a novel, and that's fun. But I really wish people wouldn't have this elitist vision of post-modernism. I think it's actually very democratic, very nice, very human. We have just gotten over the idea that we're always going up. I think that's a very healthy idea. And we have to learn to accept that there are many ways to live life, that there are many truths, and that we are all legit, and that's really nice.

I think postmodernism is a very nice and intuitive philosophy of life that we actually share, and a lot of people agree with. It's just that it's very easy to attack postmodernism because of a few individuals who have gone too far with it. I will try to explain my understanding of it. It has many implications, so I'll just pick one of them.

In modernism, there is a belief that the language we use to describe a particular phenomenon is very close to the reality that we are actually looking at. That is, the words we use to describe it reflect the underlying reality. And that is very important in science. But in humanities, social sciences, art, music, architecture, in many fields, we have a tendency to look at the world through a very specific lens. And that lens is language. So we describe things in words, and the words are chosen very carefully, and that determines how we see the world. The reality itself, as seen by us, is not as clear as we would like to see it. We see it through the language, and language changes over time. So postmodernism is a response to that. It's saying, let's just forget about what is the underlying reality, because we can never know it for sure. And let's focus on how we describe the world. And as we describe the world in a particular way, we are actually creating it. We are creating a new world, a new reality, by describing it. And that's fine. And I think that's a very healthy response to the modernism and to all the conceptions of progress and the inherent meaning of life. Because if you think about it, if you try to tell a story that has an inherent meaning to it, it becomes very, very rigid, and it becomes very, very easy to criticize and to attack. Because reality is not rigid. Reality is messy. Reality is very unpredictable and very chaotic. And if you describe it in a way that is rigid, it's not a very good description of reality. And so we are actually, I think, very postmodern in the sense that we describe things in many ways. We are aware that our description is not the only one, and we are also aware that language shapes our reality. We are aware that if we use particular words, we will see the world in a particular way. For example, if you describe someone who is nice, but you also say that they're naive, you're describing a person who is not a nice person. You're describing a person who is very gullible. But if you describe the person as nice, but very spontaneous, then you're describing a very different person. And this is how we actually speak, and we use that to shape the reality around us. And I think this is very important to understand, and this is the postmodern view. It's just that some people take it to the extreme and say, I don't care about the reality at all. Reality doesn't matter. We can just create any world we want. And I think that's very unfortunate. And I think that's the reason why postmodernism is so attacked. But I think that it's still a very healthy approach.

items.raw: Theoretically a pyramid scheme does work, in the sense that the people at the top of the pyramid do make money. And it works until a certain point, that it doesn't work anymore. So the problem with pyramid schemes is that you need an exponential growth in the number of participants for the scheme to continue to work. In a pyramid scheme, you don't actually make money, or at least in the most typical of these schemes, you don't make money by selling a product. Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp's visualisations are a thing of beauty and a bit of a mystery in their implementation but in essence they are using Fast Fourier Transforms. So they're taking the audio signal, which is in the time domain, and converting it to the frequency domain. And then they just draw the bars for the different frequencies. And they do that by basically taking the magnitude of the frequency, and then scaling it to the height of the bar, and then drawing that bar. So that's very straightforward. That's what every spectrum analyser in the world does. But the interesting thing is, for the other visualisations, which are more interesting, like the 3D ones, they actually take the raw audio signal and they just do maths on it. So they just take the waveform and they take the average, the peaks, and they use that to generate the visualisation. So for example, in the nice 3D space visualisation, it's basically drawing a sphere, and then it's just moving the vertex in and out based on the amplitude of the signal. It's actually a pretty simple algorithm. But there's a bunch of tricks they use to make it look nice, to make it look smooth, to make it look pretty. They're doing a lot of smoothing of the signal. So they're not just moving the vertex directly based on the signal, they're doing some exponential smoothing, so it's not jumping around. And then they're doing some normalisation, so that it doesn't just move in and out too much, or too little. And they're doing some fancy stuff with the colours, so it looks nice. But the actual computation of the FFT, for example, is probably the hardest part. And there are very efficient FFT algorithms, so they don't need to do it on every sample of the audio. They can just do it on a chunk of samples, say 1024 samples or 2048 samples, and then they can compute the FFT of that chunk, and then they can draw the visualisation for the next frame. And so it's quite efficient. But the rendering of the 3D visualisations, that's a bit more expensive. So they're using OpenGL, and they're using some shaders to make it look nice, and they're doing some antialiasing and some tricks to make it look good. But it's still pretty simple, in the end. It's not using ray tracing or anything fancy like that. It's just drawing polygons and moving the vertices around, and using some nice colours and lighting, and that's it. And that's why Winamp visualisations are so iconic and so cool. They look really nice, and they're very easy to generate, so they don't use too much CPU, and they work on very old hardware. And that's why they're so famous, and they're still used by a lot of people today, even in modern software.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp's visualizations are actually a historical curiosity, because they are pretty primitive by today's standards. They are mostly just ringtone or beat detectors and spectrum analysis, but pretty crude stuff. There's no true beat detection, it's more just detection of changes in the amplitude of the audio. They just assume if it goes up and down and above a certain threshold, then it's a beat. That's all. And the spectrum analysis, the Fourier transform, is done in software, and it's a simple DFT, a discrete Fourier transform, which is very inefficient in terms of computation, compared to a FFT, a fast Fourier transform. And then they just display it. So it's really not a very sophisticated visualization. And the most typical one that people use is the scope, the spectrum analyzer, the one that has the little bars that go up and down, or the rainbow scope. And that's just a very simple spectrum analyzer that will show you the frequency content of the audio. It's just one of the most basic things you can do in DSP, signal processing. And the reason why it's really pretty popular is that the spectrum analyzer is pretty easy to understand. It's easy to intuit what's going on. That the bars are higher for frequencies where there are more energy, more amplitude. And then when it hits a bass note, you see the low frequencies, the low bars going up. So it's really just a frequency content analyzer, an amplitude analyzer, a spectrum analyzer. The other visualizations are the ones that look more fancy, the 3D ones, the radar one, the galaxy one, the fishbowl one, whatever. But all of them are just very simple representations of the spectrum analyzer. The radar one, it's just a polar coordinate representation of the spectrum analyzer, where the angle is the frequency and the radius is the amplitude. The galaxy is the same, it's a 3D representation of the same thing, just that the frequency is the angle and the radius is the amplitude. So it's just the spectrum analyzer displayed in a different way. So it's all pretty basic. And that's why the Winamp visualizations are actually still in use today, in a way. Because it's simple to implement, it's simple to understand, it's not very heavy on the CPU. The DFT, the discrete Fourier transform, is very inefficient, but the frequency range is small. It's only 20 Hz to 18 kHz, and it's divided in 48 bins, so it's not a lot of computation. So it's something that you can do easily on a low-end processor. Whereas, for example, a FFT would require much more computation, much more memory. So it's really just very simple visualizations. And that's why people like them, because it's very easy to read. And also, the fact that they are displayed in the little window in Winamp, which is a nice design, makes it really really good for a bit of visualization. So it's all pretty basic, but it works.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp's visualizations are generally speaking in the class of what I would call DSP, digital signal processing. The way they work is that Winamp reads the audio stream, it decodes it, and then has the visualization take in the audio stream as it decodes it. And in a separate thread, it analyzes the audio stream and creates a representation of the audio, or the frequency spectrum or whatever. And then that representation is transferred back to the visualization thread, which renders it to the screen. So there is a very good separation between the audio thread that does the analysis and the visualization thread that does the rendering. And the analysis is the important part, because that is what determines how the visualization looks. And what the analysis is, is the FFT, the fast Fourier transform. The FFT is a numerical algorithm that decomposes a signal into its frequencies. It's the way we see sound in frequency domain. So the visualization takes the signal, say, in one second, and it analyzes that second in frequency domain, and it does that in real time. So it says, ok, for this second, the energy at this frequency is this much, and at this frequency it is this, and so on. And then it creates a spectrum, or a histogram of the frequencies, and that's what the visualization is. And that's the basis of almost all visualizations, or most visualizations. There are some exceptions where it's not FFT-based, like the oscilloscope, for example, where it doesn't need to do FFT, it just draws the waveform, the time domain waveform. But the most interesting visualizations are the ones that use FFT, and that's the spectrum analyzer, or the ones that do something more interesting with it. So Winamp, the original, had the scope, and it had the spectrum analyzer, and it had a few other visualizations, and you could load new ones. And they were all FFT-based. Then people started writing more and more visualizations, and they became very elaborate. Some of them didn't really use the FFT in the same way, but they used it as a basis. So they used the FFT as an input, and then they did something with the FFT. For example, the fishbowl visualization, or the synesthesia one, they were more interesting. They took the FFT and they transformed it into something else, like a 3D object, or some blobs or something. But the basis was always the FFT. So the FFT is the essential part of the visualization. And then there is the rendering, which is just drawing it to the screen. And for example, the spectrum analyzer, it's just drawing a bar for each frequency, and that's it. Very simple. But then when it gets more complex, it gets more interesting.

At 3:17 a.m., the bakery was all yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first loaves into the oven and found it again: a worn paperback, *The Borrowers*, resting in the wicker basket by the back door.
